site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Ambarisha's Unshaken Heart
body: In the holy city of Ayodhya, King Ambarisha observed a careful Ekadasi fast, waiting for the proper Dwadashi hour to break it. When the proud sage Durvasa arrived hungry, the king welcomed him and offered food, trusting in devotion's gentle order.

Durvasa lingered past the sacred moment, and Ambarisha sipped only water to honor his vow. Enraged, the sage conjured a fiery demon to destroy him, but from the king's heart rose the Sudarshana discus, blazing and bright, scattering the demon and turning toward Durvasa himself.

The sage fled to Brahma, to Shiva, and finally to Lord Vishnu, yet none could stay the discus. Guided to humility, Durvasa bowed before Ambarisha, who folded his hands and called the weapon home. The king stood unharmed, his steady devotion gently vindicated.

stories.title: Prahlada's Quiet Faith Triumphs
body: Young Prahlada, son of the proud asura king Hiranyakashipu, was sent to the teachers Shanda and Amarka because he would not stop speaking the praises of Vishnu. When asked what he had learned, he answered gently that the highest teaching was to serve the Lord who dwells in the heart of every being.

His father, enraged, ordered him destroyed by trampling elephants, fire, poison, serpents, and a fall from a cliff, yet Prahlada emerged unharmed from every trial. At last the tyrant pointed to a pillar of his own court and demanded the boy prove whether Vishnu could be found even there.

When the king struck the pillar, the Lord appeared as Narasimha, half-man and half-lion, and delivered justice to the tyrant. Peaceful Prahlada was installed as king of the asuras, his quiet devotion vindicated, and his father's pride dissolved in the radiant presence of the divine.

stories.title: Sixteen Forever, Held in Light
body: The young sage Markandeya was born beneath a starry sky heavy with ill omens, and the fates had whispered that his life would end at sixteen. When that hour finally arrived, the boy did not weep or run. He walked to the shrine, wrapped his arms around the lingam of Shiva, and began to chant the holy names with all the breath in his small body.

Soon Yama, the god of death, came gliding through the stillness, his dark attendants at his heels, casting his noose toward the sage. The loop slipped past Markandeya and caught instead upon the lingam he embraced. From the sacred pillar a terrible form burst forth, scattering the messengers of death and driving Yama himself back into the shadows, his errand undone.

Pleased by such unwavering love, the lord declared that Markandeya would remain sixteen forever, untouched by death's claim. The sage lifted his head, his heart renewed, and continued his worship with quiet joy, knowing that sincere devotion had turned even the appointed hour into a doorway of grace.

stories.title: The Squirrel at Rama's Bridge
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 4 (popular tradition; see also Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda background)
body: On the shore where Rama's vanara army gathered to build a bridge to Lanka, great bears hauled boulders and dragged tree trunks to the water's edge. Among them darted a small squirrel, rushing back and forth with a single grain of sand, then rolling in the shallows so that sparkles clung to her fur before she dashed to add them to the causeway.

The general Neela laughed at her tiny labor, but Rama gently lifted the little creature into his hands and soothed her earnest heart. He stroked her back with three fingers, and those soft marks stayed upon her forever, his quiet praise for every sincere offering, however small.

With the devotion of the squirrel joined to the strength of the great boulders, the bridge reached across the sea and the army crossed to Lanka. The smallest helper walked home honored, her humble effort woven into a victory made whole by Rama's gentle compassion.

stories.title: The King Who Weighed Himself for a Dove
stories.source: Sibi Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell (ed.), 1901
body: In the ancient kingdom of the Sibis, a trembling dove fled into King Sibi's open court, a fierce hawk hard behind it. Refusing to betray any refugee, the king stepped between them, offering instead his own flesh, weighed piece by piece against the small frightened bird upon the balance.

But every portion he laid down only made the dove seem heavier, and at last Sibi climbed onto the scale himself, giving his whole body for the life that had trusted him. The hawk's fierce form shimmered and dissolved, revealed as Sakka, the god who had come to test the heart of the realm.

Pleased by such steadfast compassion, Sakka restored King Sibi whole and unblemished, then set the dove softly free. The court rejoiced, and the kingdom of the Sibis was praised across the land for a mercy so complete it bent even the gods to honor.
